summary:
SismoView turns complex satellite and earthquake data into a story people can explore. Built around a Venezuela earthquake case study, it guides users from a 3D view of the region to an interactive dashboard where they can compare NISAR radar observations, including coherence, phase, and ground displacement.

Our goal is to make scientific data easier to understand without oversimplifying it. We bring maps and measurements together, explain what they show, and are transparent about their limits. Real observations are presented with context; when something is an interpretation or hypothesis, we label it as such rather than presenting it as fact.

By making these distinctions clear, SismoView helps people engage with Earth-observation data, ask better questions, and understand how evidence can inform further investigation. The experience is available in English and Spanish.

details:
SismoView: Following the clues left by an earthquake

SismoView is an interactive web application that brings together satellite maps, seismic data, and 3D visualizations to explore a case study in Venezuela. Rather than leaving measurements scattered across files and charts, it starts with a simple question: What may have changed on the surface near the epicenters?

How does it work, and what can you explore?

The experience begins with an introduction to the NISAR satellite, then takes users on a guided tour of a 3D globe and an analytical dashboard. There, they can locate the earthquakes in the case study—Yunare, magnitude 7.5, and San Felipe, magnitude 7.2 and compare different data layers: phase fringes, radar line-of-sight (LOS) displacement, image coherence, deformation components, and radar backscatter observations.

The dashboard also includes seismic charts and contextual maps. Users can move from a broad view of the region to a closer look at the observed signals, without needing advanced expertise to start exploring.

What benefits and impact does the project aim for?

The project aims to make Earth observation and seismic analysis more accessible. By bringing maps, measurements, and explanations together in one place, it helps people understand what satellite data can reveal and how those observations relate to a specific region. Its intended impact is educational: to spark curiosity about science, make evidence easier to explore, and communicate complex phenomena more clearly and visually.

What did we use to build it?

The application is built with React and TypeScript. It uses Cesium for the 3D globe, Leaflet for maps, and Recharts for charts. Satellite and geographic products are prepared with Python scripts using tools such as NumPy, h5py, and rasterio. A JavaScript script is also used to calculate coherence metrics. All data used comes from real NASA datasets.

The project does not build hardware or operate a satellite; it works with NISAR observation products and other data from the case study. To explore the application, users just need a computer and a web browser.

This experience was designed for laptops and desktop computers, for the best experience, we recommend using a laptop.

What makes the project creative?

SismoView turns data exploration into a visual and sound-rich journey. It combines a space-inspired look, a guided introduction, interactive maps, and controls for comparing data layers. It also features sound effects, music, and audio tracks created by the team at home to make the experience more immersive and help users feel fully engaged as they explore.

When designing the project, we considered how to make the data easy to navigate and understand. We focused on clear sources and measurements, signal quality, performance, and access in both Spanish and English.
